options: The sensitivity of option value to volatility
The sensitivity of option value to the passage of time
The sensitivity of option value to a $1 change in the underlying's price
The sensitivity of option value to the risk-free rate
questions.explain: Delta is ∂V/∂S, the option's sensitivity to a change in the underlying price. Call delta ranges 0 to 1 (N(d1)); put delta ranges -1 to 0 (N(d1)-1).

questions.q: Why is Gamma important to a dealer who has delta-hedged a short option position?
options: Gamma has no practical relevance to hedging
Gamma measures how fast Delta itself changes as the stock moves, meaning a delta-neutral hedge drifts out of balance and must be rebalanced
Gamma tells you the option's time to expiration
Gamma is only relevant for European options, not American options
questions.explain: Delta is a snapshot that changes as the stock price moves — Gamma quantifies that rate of change, which is why high-gamma positions require frequent rehedging.

questions.q: A long call option has delta 0.6, and the stock rises by $2. Approximately how much does the call's value increase, holding other inputs fixed?
questions.explain: Delta approximates the dollar change in option value per $1 move in the stock: 0.6 * $2 = $1.20.

questions.q: Which statement about Theta is correct for a long option position (call or put)?
options: Theta is typically positive, meaning the option gains value just from time passing
Theta is typically negative, meaning the option loses value from time decay as expiration approaches, all else equal
Theta is always exactly zero for at-the-money options
Theta only applies to American options
questions.explain: Theta = ∂V/∂t is typically negative for long options: as time passes with no favorable move in the underlying, time value erodes.

questions.q: Why do both a long call and a long put have positive Vega?
options: Because they are both unaffected by volatility
Because higher volatility widens the range of possible future outcomes, which increases the value of the right to benefit only from favorable outcomes while being protected from unfavorable ones
Because Vega is only defined for calls, not puts
Because higher volatility always reduces the risk-free rate
questions.explain: Options have asymmetric, capped-downside payoffs, so more uncertainty (volatility) in the underlying raises their value whether they're calls or puts — hence positive Vega for both.
